Foreword
Dated : 22nd June, 2010
Lucknow
Although India is the largest mango producer in the world, the productivity 
is considerably low. One of the major reasons of low productivity is the occurrence 
of diseases on the crop causing huge losses every year both at pre and post-harvest 
stages, limiting profitability to the growers. Diverse climatic conditions prevalent 
in the country predispose the crop to incidence of over 140 pathogens causing 
damages of varying intensities to the crop at different stages of production. Besides 
these, there are several physiological disorders that also affect mango production. 
For effective management of these diseases, it requires that they are identified and 
diagnosed properly. Keeping this in view, the present bulletin has been revised 
and updated. With dedicated research work for over three decades, pathologists of 
this Institute have standardized effective disease management schedule for all the 
major diseases and disorders of mango integrating cultural, mechanical, biological 
and chemical strategies. As diseases are sensitive at their critical periods, the most 
optimum period for their efficient control have been identified and need based 
cultural operations and suitable management interventions have been 
recommended.  
Sincere efforts of Plant Pathologists of this Institute in preparing and 
publishing this extension bulletin for the benefit of end users is highly appreciable. 
I hope that this publication will serve as a useful guide for growers, extension 
workers, teachers, students and research workers associated with mango industry. 
An appeal is made specially to the growers to adopt these schedules for effective 
management of diseases, so that pre and post-harvest losses could be minimized 
and quality mango productivity and export gets enhanced.
(H. Ravishankar)
 Director

## Page 5

Preface
A.K. Misra
B.K. Pandey
Dated : 22nd June, 2010
Lucknow
The present bulletin entitled “Integrated Disease Management 
Practices in Mango” is prepared with the aim that the major diseases 
and disorders of mango can be properly identified with the help of 
colour photographs depicting the typical symptoms and the 
descriptions described so as to render field identification easy. Only on 
the basis of proper identification, suitable control measures could be 
adopted for effective management. Considering the necessity of 
environmental safety, it is desired that only need based fungicides are 
used and hence the need of integrated disease management strategy 
was felt. On the basis of different experiments conducted during the 
last three decades at this Institute and the experiences gained, most 
suitable cultural practices, mechanical control measures, chemicals, 
biological and critical time of disease incidence and management have 
been identified and an integrated disease management schedule has 
been developed. On the basis of the disease problems of particular 
region, relevant schedules need to be adopted. The authors sincerely 
hope that it will serve as a useful reference for mango growers, 
extension workers, teachers, research scholars and students of Plant 
Pathology associated with mango production.

Introduction
The mango (Mangifera indica L.) is an
important fruit crop of tropical and
subtropical countries of the world. It is
grown in at least 87 countries but no.
where it is so greatly valued as in India.
India is the largest producer of mango in
the world accounting for 42.10 per cent
of the total mango production. The
mango accounts for 38 per cent of total
area under fruits and 18.6 per cent of total
fruit production in the country during the
year 2008-09. Although India is the largest
producer of mango, but in terms of
productivity, it ranks lower in the list. The
low productivity is due to the wide range
of climatic conditions and environmental
situations in which it is grown and the
diversity of the associated disease
problems. Over 140 pathogens are known
to cause damage to the crop, but there
are only a few diseases which are of great
economic importance. The main diseases
and disorders which cause great loss are
described in brief in this bulletin with their
management practices.
The mango crop is affected by a
number of diseases at all stages of its
development, right from the plants in the
nursery to the fruits in transit and storage.
Almost every part viz. stem, branch, twig,
root, leaf, petiole, flower and fruit are
affected by various pathogens. These
diseases manifest themselves as several
kinds of rots, die back, mildew, necrosis,
scab, blotch, stem bleeding, wilt, spots,
canker, mould, malformation, etc. Some
of these diseases cause heavy loss and
have become limiting factor in mango
cultivation in some regions. Powdery
mildew, anthracnose, die back, sooty
mould, gummosis, malformation, black
tip and internal necrosis cause great l oss
to the orchardists in India. Field
identification, symptoms, integrated
control and calendar of operations during
different months for the management of
some of the important diseases are
enumerated in this bulletin.
Powdery Mildew
[Oidium mangiferae Berthet.]
Symptoms
The symptoms can be noticed on the
inflorescence, stalk of the inflorescence,
leaves and young fruits. The characteristic
symptom of the disease is white
superficial powdery growth of the fungus
on these parts having millions of conidia
which are borne in chains on
conidiophores. The disease spreads
through air borne conidia.
On leaves
Infection is frequently noticed on
young leaves, when their colour changes
from brown to light green. Young leaves
are attacked on both sides as small
irregular greyish patches, but on the
underside the symptoms are generally
more conspicuous. Often, these patches
coalesce and occupy larger areas turning
into purplish brown in colour. At a later
stage, patches become darker in colour.
Under favourable environmental
conditions, invaded areas are covered
with a luxuriant whitish growth,
consisting of mycelial mat and conidia.
The pathogen is frequently restricted to
the area of the central and lateral veins
of infected leaves and such leaves often
twist, curl and get distorted. Recently, it
has been observed that while distortion
of leaves is more common in plains, in the
foot hill areas, it shows ashy brown
patches with white powdery growth on
the leaf surface.

## Page 8

2
On inflorescence
Main symptom
of powdery mildew
is observed on
inflorescence and
powdery mildew
causes more harm to
crop if infection
occurs on panicles.
Mildew pathogen
attacks flowers and
white superficial
powdery fungus
grows on the
i n f l o r e s c e n c e
resulting into its
shedding. The sepals are relatively more
susceptible than the petals. The affected
flowers fail to open and may fall
prematurely. Dropping of unfertilized
infected flowers leads to serious crop loss.
On fruits
Young fruits are covered entirely by
the white mildew growth. When it grows,
epidermis of the infected fruits cracks and
corky tissues are formed. Purplish brown
blotchy areas appear on the skin of older
fruits. Such fruits may remain on the tree
until they reach up to pea size and then
drop prematurely. Dropping of immature
fruits lead to serious crop loss.
Management
 Pruning of diseased leaves and
malformed panicles reduce the load
of primary inoculum and improve
the control achieved by spraying of
mildewcides.
 As the inflorescence infection causes
actual serious harm, 3 sprays of
fungicides during flowering season
is recommended at 15-20 days
interval.
 It has been o bserved that epidemic
of disease occur when the maximum
temperature reaches 35 0C and
minimum temperature 17 0C during
3rd and 4 th week of March in
northern plains.
 Although 3 spray schedule is
recommended for the management
of this disease, intelligent
management with one spray can be
made on the basis of forecasting of
disease.
 Critical period for PM spread is
identified during 3 rd - 4 th weak of
March in northern plains.
 First spray of wettable sulphur (0.2%)
when panicles are 10 cm in size.
 Second spray of dinocap (Karathane
0.1 %) after 15-20 days of first spray.
 Third spray of tridemorph (Calixin
0.1 %) after 15-20 days of second
spray.
Precaution: Spraying should be avoided
when flowers are in full bloom.
Anthracnose
[Colletotrichum gloeosporioides Penz.  =
Glomerella cingulata (Stons.) Spauld &
Schrenk]
Symptoms
The disease is
observed on leaves,
petioles, twigs, blossoms
and fruits.
On leaves
Characteristic symp-
toms appear as oval or
irregular vinaceous
brown to deep brown
spots of various sizes
scattered all over the leaf
surface. Under damp
condition, the fungus
Anthracnose
on leaf
Powdery mildew on
inflorescence

## Page 9

3
grows rapidly forming elongated brown
necrotic areas measuring 20-25 mm in
diameter. Later the lesions get blighted and
ruptured and show ‘shot hole’ symptom.
Young leaves (light green stage) are more
prone to attack than the older ones.
On petiole and twig
Petioles, when affected, turn grey or
black. The leaves droop down, slowly dry
up and ultimately fall-off, leaving a black
scar on the twig. Disease produces
elongated black necrotic areas on the
twigs. The tips of the very young branches
start drying from tip downwards
showing characteristic symptom of
wither tip.
On blossom
On inflorescence, the earliest
symptoms of the disease are the
production of blackish brown specks on
the peduncle and flowers. Small black
spots appear on the panicles and open
flowers, which gradually enlarge and
coalesce to cause drying of flowers. The
infected flowers fall-off, leaving the more
persistent spikes on the peduncles.
On fruit
On fruits in field, anthracnose
develops as latent infection. Very minute
spots develop which are not even visible,
but when these fruits are stored, develop
rot due to anthracnose disease. Symptom
of post harvest rot and its management
are described under post harvest diseases.
Management
 Severely infected twigs from the tree
should be pruned. Diseased leaves,
twigs and fruits, lying on the floor of
the orchard, should be collected and
burnt.
 Blossom infection can be controlled
effectively by 2 sprays of
carbendazim (Bavistin 0.1%) at 15
days interval.
 The foliar infection can be controlled
by 2 sprays of copper oxychloride
(0.3%) at the interval of 20 days.
 Pre harvest sprays with thiophanate
methyl or carbendazim (Topsin M or
Bavistin 0.1%) in the field reduce the
latent infection on fruits.
Mango Malformation
[Fusarium mangiferae ]
Malformation is of two types
(a) vegetative and (b) floral.
Symptoms
Vegetative malformation
V eg e t a t i v e
malformation is
pronounced in
young seedlings.
The affected
seedlings develop
v e g e t a t i v e
growth, which
are abnormal,
swollen and have
very short inter-
nodes. Very small
Malformation in mango tree
Vegetative malformation

## Page 10

4
narrow leaves are formed. This form
bunches of various sizes, which are often
produced on the top of the seedlings,
giving bunchy top appearance. Such
formations are also found on grown up
plants, but are relatively less.
Floral malformation
The characteristic symptom of floral
malformation is reduction in length of the
primary axis and
the secondary
branches of the
panicle which
make the flowers
appear in clusters.
The flower buds
are transformed
into vegetative
buds and a large
number of small
leaves and stems,
which are characterized by appreciably
reduced internodes and give an
appearance of witches broom. The flower
bud seldom open and remain dull green.
Some floral malformed panicles are also
of loose type. Both types of floral
malformed panicles do not produce fruits.
Management
 The floral malformed panicles/
vegetative malformed shoots should
be pruned and burnt, which reduce
the further incidence of
malformation.
 Application of NAA (200ppm) in the
first week of October followed by
deblossoming in the late December
or January reduce the incidence of
malformation.
Dieback
[Lasiodiplodia theobromae  (Pat.) Griffon &
Mouble Synonyms :  Botryodiplodia
theobromae Pat.]
Symptoms
The disease
is noticeable at
any time of the
year but it
becomes cons-
picuous during
October and
November. It is
characterised by
drying back of
twigs from top
d o w n w a r d s ,
particularly in
the older trees
followed by drying of leaves which gives
an appearance of fire scorch. Dark
patches are usually seen on young green
twigs. When the dark lesions increase in
size, dying of young twigs begin. The
upper leaves loose their green colour and
gradually dry. Internal browning in the
wood tissue is observed when it is slit open
along with the long axis. Cracks appear
on branches/twigs and
gum exudes before they
die.
When the graft
union of nursery plants
are affected, they usually
die. It has also been
noticed that the infection
occurs at nodes at
variable distances below
growing point and the
part of the twig on both
the sides of infection
die.
Foral malformation
Die back affected plant
Die back
affected twig

## Page 11

5
Management
 Pruning of twigs/branches (10-15
cm below the infection site) followed
by pasting/spraying of Bordeaux
mixture (5:5:50) or copper
oxychloride (0.3 %) on cut ends is the
most effective method for control of
the disease.
 Scion wood selected for propagation
should be selected from healthy
plants and should be free from
infection, while multiplying the
planting materials.
Gummosis
[Lasiodiplodia theobromae  (Pat.) Griffon
and Mouble Synonyms: Botryodiplodia
theobromae perfect stage Pat.  Physalospora
rhodina Cooke]
Generally those mango trees are
affected by the gummosis, which are
planted in sandy/light soil but its
prevalence has also been noticed in other
mango growing soils too. The disease
occurs on stems and branches of mango
trees. The disease is noticed after rainy
season particularly in winters.
Symptoms
 The disease is characterized by the
presence of profuse oozing of gum on the
surface of the affected wood, bark of the
trunk and also on
larger branches but
more common on
the cracked
branches. In severe
cases, droplets of
gum trickle down on
stem and bark turns
dark brown with
longitudinal cracks,
rots completely and
later the tree dries
up due to cracking, rotting and girdling
effects.
Management
 The diseased bark/portion should be
removed or cleaned and pasted with
Bordeaux paste or copper
oxychloride paste.
 Application of Copper sulphate @500
gm/tree (depending upon the age of
the tree) in soil around the tree trunk
is recommended. However, the
gummosis is very less in the orchards
receiving regular copper oxychloride
sprays for the control of leaf spot
diseases.
Phoma Blight
[Phoma glomerata  (Corda) Woll. &
Hochapf]
Symptoms
It can be differentiated from
anthracnose spots which generally occurs
on younger leaves and are round shaped
spots, while the spots of phoma blight are
angular in shape and are noticed on
matured/old leaves only. Initially, the
lesions are minute, irregular, yellow to
light brown coloured, scattered all over
the leaf lamina. As the lesions enlarge,
their colour changes from brown to
Pasting of copper paste on cut ends for
management of dieback
Gumosis

## Page 12

6
cinnamon, and
these become
irregular in shape.
Fully developed
spots are
characterised by
dark margin and
dull grey necrotic
centres. In severe
cases, the spots
coalesce to form
big patches which
result in withering and defoliation of
infected leaves. Such plants can be
identified easily from a distance with less
foliage. Disease is more severe in the
months of November to January.
Management
 As nutrition plays an important role,
balanced nutrition provides
resistance against Phoma blight.
 Spraying of benomyl (0.2%) or
copper oxychloride (0.3%)
(2 spraying at the interval of 15 days)
has been found effective against this
disease.
Sooty Mould
In India, the disease is
caused by Capnodium
mangiferae Cke. and
Borwn, Microxyphium
columnatum, Leptoxyphium
fumago , Tripospermum
myrti, etc. Since, these fungi
do not sporulate on the
plant and they are often
found in combination with
one another, it is difficult to
identify the specific species
which are involved on a
given leaf.
Symptoms
The disease is characterized by the
presence of a black velvety thin
membraneous covering on the leaves,
stems and fruits. These range from thin,
diffused webs of dark hyphae to opaque
felty layers. The mycelium of these fungi
are superficial and do not penetrate the
host tissue. In severe cases, the tree appear
black from the distance due to heavy
infection. Because of the production of
masses of black mycelium/spores, which
stick on the leaf surface due to sticky
‘honey dew’, the foliage appears black,
ugly and hence the name ‘sooty mould’
is given. The severity of incidence depends
upon the sugary secretion by insects.
During flowering time if the fungus infects
the blossoms, the fruit setting is also
affected and at times even small fruits
drop. Mature fruits having black patches
specially on shoulder region detract
considerably the appearance and
marketability of fruits.
Management
 The orchards  in which proper
management of hopper scale/mealy
bug is done, do not develop sooty
mould.
 If honey dew secreting insects (scale
insects, hoppers and mealy bugs) are
controlled properly by suitable
insecticides, the mould dies out for
want of a suitable growth medium.
 Spraying of starch @ 2% is effective
in controlling the disease.
 Spraying of Wettable sulphur +
Dimethoate + Gum Acacia (0.2 + 0.05
+ 0.06% respectively), control sooty
mould.
 Two to three  sprays of Indian oil
Phoma blight
Sooty mould

## Page 13

7
formulation No.1 & 2 (3%) at 15 days
interval control the disease.
 Care should be taken that
application of pesticides should cover
both the surfaces of leaves.
Scab
[Elsinoe mangiferae Bitancourt and Jenkins
= anamorph: Sphaceloma mangiferae
(Bitancourt and Jenkins)].
Symptoms
The scab
fungus attacks
leaves, panicles,
blossoms, twigs,
bark of stems
and mango
fruits. Spots are
circular, slightly
angular, elongated, 2-4 mm in diameter,
brown but during rainy season, lesions
differ in size, shape and colour. Symptoms
produced by the disease are very much
like those of anthracnose. On leaves, the
spots are smaller
than a nthracnose
infection and the
surface is covered
with a delicate
velvety down.
Severe attack
causes crinkling
and distortion of
the leaves,
followed by
p r e m a t u r e
shedding. Larger
spots on young leaves are greyish in colour
surrounded by narrow dark border.
Commonly the centre wither away
leaving irregular shot holes. The blotches
on the stem bark are greyish and irregular
in shape.
On young fruits, the infection spots
are grey to greyish brown with dark
irregular margins. As the fruit attains in
size, spots also enlarge and the centre may
become covered with crack fissure and
corky tissues. Conidia of the fungus are
produced on the fruit surface until it
reaches maturity.
Management
 Frequent spray of copper
oxycholoride (0.3%) are effective to
protect new flushes of growth from
scab in nurseries.
Black Banded
[Rhinocladium corticolum Massee, perfect
stage Peziotrichum corticolum  (Massee)
Subramanian]
Symptoms
The disease is
noticed on the
midribs/veins of the
leaves, twigs and
branches of mango
as black velvety
fungal growth. The
incidence of disease
is very low on the
main branches.
Recently, the disease
was reported in
severe form in
Gujarat on main branches too. It presents
a characteristic and conspicuous black
banded appearance and thus considered
appropriate to name it as ‘Black banded’
disease. The infected portions of the bark
usually show valvety mycelial growth
and clusters of conidiophores. The
mycelial growth drops off in the summer
months leaving light black bands at the
affected portions. The fungus is confined
to the upper layer of the bark.
Scab on fruit
Scab on leaves
Black banded

## Page 14

8
Management
 Gunny rubbing on twigs/branches to
remove the black growth and then
application of Bordeaux paste and
spraying of Bordeaux mixture 5:5:50
or copper oxychloride (0.3%) control
the disease.
Root Rot and Damping Off
[Rhizoctonia solani  Kühn, teleomorph :
Thanatephorus cucumeris  (Frank) Donk]
Symptoms
The disease is
characterised by
sudden dropping of
leaves after the
emergence of
seedlings from the
soil. During
prolonged rainy
and humid
weather, infection
occurs at/or below
the ground level
with circular to irregular water-soaked
patches. These patches enlarge and
ultimately girdle the entire base of the
plant. On account of rotting, the diseased
tissues become soft, dark brown or black
and the entire seedling collapse and dies.
Fungal mycelia and sclerotia are densely
present on the severely infected parts.
Rotting may spread both above and below
the stem down up to the roots resulting
into disintegration and the plant dies.
Management
 Care should be taken that water
should not stag nate near the root
zone.
 Nursery should be raised on elevated
beds.
 Nursery beds should be fumigated
before sowing.
 Application of Trichoderma sp. in the
affected nursery is effective.
 During the growing season,
Bordeaux mixture (1.5%) should be
sprayed on the plants and the soil at
weekly intervals.
Bacterial Canker
[Xanthomonas campestris pv. Mangiferae
indicae (Patel, Moniz & Kulkarni) Robbs,
Ribiero & Kimura]
Symptoms
The disease is noticed on leaves, leaf
stalks, stem, twigs, branches and fruits.
On leaves
On leaves, minute water soaked,
irregular, stellate to angular, raised
lesions, measuring 1-4 mm in diameter are
formed. These lesions are light yellow in
colour, initially with yellow halo but with
age, enlarge or coalesce to form irregular
dark brown necrotic cankerous patches
usually on the lower side but occasionally
on both sides. On
young leaves, the
halos are larger and
distinct, while on
older leaves, these are
narrow and could be
observed only against
light. Under severe
infections, leaves turn
yellow and get
dropped off. Canker
on leaf stalks,
sometimes progress
superficially along
with midrib.
Root rot
Bacterial canker on
leaves

## Page 15

9
On twigs and branc hes
On twigs, branches and stem freshly
developed lesions are observed as water
soaked, dark brown, raised with
longitudinal fissures exposing the
vascular tissues mostly filled with gummy
substance which oozes outward. The
infections are deep seated. Black
discolouration of underlying tissues with
cracked bark are also characteristic
symptoms.
On fruits
On fruits,
symptoms are
quite conspicuous.
Water soaked,
dark brown to
black coloured
lesions are
observed, which
gradually develop
into cankerous,
raised or flat
spots. These spots
grow bigger
usually up to 5
mm in diameter, which covers almost the
whole fruit. These spots often, burst
extruding gummy substances containing
highly contagious bacterial cells.
Sometimes, the exposed flesh in
cankerous spots attract insects and
subsequently involved by secondary
microorganisms, which initiates rotting.
Fruit dropping was observed to be more
when cankers develop near the stalk end.
Severely infected fruits crack and become
brown in colour. In some excessive
infected fruits, pulp and stones are also
found i nfected.
Management
 Regular inspection of orchards and
sanitation are recommended as
preventive measures against the
disease. The diseased fruits/twigs/
leaves should be collected and
destroyed (burnt or placed under
soil).
 Selection of stones from healthy
fruits for root stock is advisable.
 Three sprays of streptocyclines (200
ppm) at 10 days intervals reduce the
leaf/fruit infection.
 Streptocycline (300 ppm) along with
copper oxychloride (0.3%) is found
more effective, if incidence is severe.
Red Rust
(Cephaleuros virescens Kunze)
Symptoms
The disease is readily recognised by
the presence of the rusty red fructification
of the alga on the surface of the leaves,
veins, petiole and young twigs. Initially,
the spots are greenish grey in colour and
velvety in texture, which finally turn into
reddish brown in colour. Spots are
circular to irregular in shape, erumpent,
Bacterial canker on fruit
and stone
Red rust Red rust scar after
shedding of spores

## Page 16

10
measuring 2 mm in diameter. When these
spots coalesce, they may be up to 1 cm in
diameter. After shedding of spores, the
algal matrix remains attached to the leaf
surface, leaving a creamy white mark at
the original rust spot.
Management
 If vigour of the plant is maintained
by balanced nutrients, the disease
occurrence is less.
 Bordeaux mixture (5:5:50) and
copper oxychloride (0.3%) for the
control of algal disease are effective.
 As the disease starts on the onset of
rain, it is desired to spray fungicide
twice during the month of July at 15
days interval.
Lichens
[Strigula elegans (Fee.) Mull. Arg.]
Symptoms
Lichens are found on full grown
trees of mango, mainly on trunks,
branches and twigs in the areas of high
humidity, heavy rainfall and poorly
managed orchards. It is seen in the form
of whitish, pinkish, superficial patches of
different shapes on the main trunk,
branches, leaves and twigs of the trees.
In general, trees with severe lichen
intensity show, poor growth. Lichens do
not damage trees directly but give them
an ugly look and unhealthy appearance.
Management
 Field sanitation and balanced
nutrition help in checking the
disease.
 The lichens can be managed by
gunny rubbing followed by spraying
the trunk, branches, twigs with
commercial Caustic Soda (1.0%).
Frost Injury
Symptoms
Symptoms of frost injury in mango
trees are characterized in the form of
spliting of bark, which may not be visible
at intial stages but one can visualize it only
when the plants start withering away.
Exudation of gum from the stem bark,
death of new shoots, charred appearance
of leaves, burning of growing flower buds
and panicles, complete death of plants,
are the symptoms which have been
noticed as indicative of frost injury to a
mango plant.
Lichen on stem Lichen on leaves

Management
 To protect the young mango plants
from the frost, plants should be
thatched with dried grass. The plants
are covered on all sides, except east,
to allow penetration of sunlight and
air.
 Irrigation of plants during frost
period saves plant from frost injury.
Sprinkler irrigation and overhead
irrigation are effective during cold
spells.
 Grove heaters are effective for
protecting the tops of both old and
young trees during cold spells.
Black Tip
(Physiological disorder)
Symptoms
Black tip is generally observed in the
orchards, which are located near the
vicinity of brick
kilns. Symptoms
become visible
when the mango
fruits attain some
size. Small
aetiolated area
develops near the
distal end of the
fruit which
gradually spreads, turns nearly black and
covers the tip of the fruit completely. The
black area remains hard and the growth
of the fruit is checked. In some varieties
viz.  Dashehari, there is tapering and
intensification of green colour at the distal
end. The growth of the fruit is also
checked. The disease is characterized by
the appearance of two, three or more
small isolated aetiolated areas towards the
distal end of the fruit in sinus region.
Management
 The incidence of black tip of mango
can be minimized by the spray of
borax (1%). The first spray should be
done positively at pea stage followed
by two more sprays at 15 days
interval.
 Planting of mango orchard in north-
south direction and 5-6 km away
from the brick kilns reduce the
incidence of black tip to a greater
extent.
 The chimni height should be
increased if the brick kilns are near
the mango orchard.

[Physiological disorder]
Symptoms
First, water
soaked greyish
spots develop
on the lower
side of the fruit.
Later, the spots
enlarge and
develop into
dark brown
necrotic area. The internal tissue start
disintegrating and the pericarp and
mesocarp is disintegrated exposing the

tissue, which gives an appearance of
rotting of tissue.  Yellow coloured droplets
come out. Stone also show browning.
Affected fruits drop easily.
Management
 The incidence of internal necrosis can
be minimized by the application of
borax at the rate of 500g/tree in the

followed by two more sprays at 15

Mango Fruit Clustering
This abnormality is characterized by
formation of several fruitlets at the tip of
panicle. The fruitlets are darker green in
colour and
their shape
is slightly
curved than
the normal
fruits. These
f r u i t s
g e n e r a l l y
hang for
more time
compared to some normal fruits, which
subsequently drop due to other fruit drop
reasons. Retention of these fruitlets for
longer period gives a general impression
that there will be good fruit set. However,
these fruitlets do not grow more and later
drop. The fruits do not have formation of
seeds.
Management
 During flower opening stage, spray
of insecticides and fungicides should
be avoided.
 Population of pollinators should be
kept more during flowering season.
Chloride Toxicity
Symptoms
The main symptom of the chloride
toxicity is that the leaves start drying from
the tip which increases along the margins
giving tip burning appearance. Dried
portion shows brick red colour. The
symptoms are so distinct that the plants
can be spotted out easily even from a
distance.
Management
 Fertilizers containing chloride should
be substituted with muriate of
potash sulphate.
 Application of fungicide, copper
oxychloride should be avoided.
 Fallen leaves should be collected and
removed from field.
Post Harvest Fruit Rots
Anthracnose
[Colletotrichum gloeosporioides  Penz. =
Glomerella cingulata  (Stons.) Spauld &
Schrenk]
Symptoms
The post harvest infection starts from
the field as latent infection. On stored

## Page 19

13
fruits, black spots are produced. Initially
the spots are round but later coalesce to
form large irregular blotches. Sometimes,
it covers the entire fruit surface. The spots
have large deep cracks in which fungus
penetrates deep into the fruit, causing
extensive rotting. Under moist conditions,
the blackened areas become covered with
minute pinkish reproductive bodies of the
fungus. Staining, russetting and tear
streaking, involving only the skin of the
fruit, are attributed to the same fungus.
Management
 The major strategies in controlling
post harvest anthracnose are
scheduled preharvest sprays with
thiophanate methyl or carbendazim
(Topsin M or Bavistin 0.1%) in the
field to reduce the latent infection
and treatment of the fruits with hot
water alone or hot water with
fungicides after harvest to eradicate
the left over latent infection. Hot
water treatment alone at 52±1 0C for
30 minutes gives good control of
anthracnose. However, the duration
of hot water treatment can be
reduced to 15 minutes by
supplementing it with fungicides,
viz. , carbendazim or thiophanate
methyl (Bavistin or Topsin M 0.05%).
Stem end rot
[Diplodia natalensis  Pole Evans]
Symptoms
The disease
starts on fruit at
the base of the
pedicel. A circular
brown area
develops near the
stem end, which
gradually starts
developing as
dark brown to
black area
towards the lower portion of the fruit and
later even cover the entire fruit surface.
The rotting is so fast that the entire fruit
rots within 2-3 days. The disease may start
on fruit from some point other than the
stem end, when fruit gets bruises. The
disease is observed on ripe fruits only.
Management
 Pre harvest spray of carbendazim or
thiophanate methyl (Bavistin or
Topsin M 0.1%) 15 days before
harvesting control the post harvest
rot due to stem end rot.
 As the disease starts from the stem
end, it is desired that the harvesting
of fruits is done carefully. If the fruits
are harvested along with 5cm stalk,
the disease is checked. If fruits are
harvested without stalk, the opening
should be closed with wax.
 Disease can be controlled by
dipping the fruits in hot water 52±l0C
with 0.05% carbendazim for five
minutes.

Black rot
[Aspergillus niger  Van Tiegh]
Symptoms
Affected fruits
show characteristic
yellowing with irregular
dull greyish spots,
which develop into black
necrotic area with
growth of black mould.
Tissues below and
around the spots
disintegrate and emit
foul odour. The fruits rot
very fast. The rotting may start from any
point but injury is essential for the start
of rot. It may also start from the stem end
as there remains natural opening.
Management
 It is desired that the harvesting of
fruits is done carefully as any injury
to fruit predisposes it to the attack of
Aspergillus rot.
 Fruits should not be allowed to touch
soil.
 Fruit harvesting and handling should
be done carefully in clean manner.
 Disease can be controlled by dipping
fruits in hot water 52± 1 0C with
0.05% carbendazim for five minutes.
Calendar of Operations for the
Integrated Disease Management in
Mango
On the basis of the above control
measures, a systematic programme is
prepared month-wise so that all the
important diseases are tackled in an
integrated man ner.
January
 To protect plants from frost injury, it
is necessary to irrigate the field
during this month.
 Young plants should be protected by
thatching the plants. Care should be
taken that the east side of the thatch
is kept open so that the sun light
enters in the thatch at least for some
time in the morning.
 For the control of mango
malformation new flower buds or
new growing panicles should be
deblossomed.
February
 Powdery mildew affected leaves and
malformed panicles should be
removed and burnt.
 First spray for the control of powdery
mildew is done with wettable
sulphur @ 2g / liter. Liquid soap is
mixed with the solution so that the
fungicide sticks well and make the
fungicide more effective. Generally,
10-20 liters of solution is required for
one plant (10-15 old plant),
depending upon its age.
March
 For the control of powdery mildew
second spray is done with
Tridemorph (Calixin @ 0.1% i.e.
1ml/liter). Care should be taken that
the second spray is done before the
opening of the flowers.
 In the third or fourth week of the
month, Dinocap or Tridemefon
(Karathane or Bayleton @ 0.1% i.e.
1ml, 1g/liter) is sprayed. Third spray
should be done when fruit set has
already taken place.
 During this month, infestation of
Aspergillus rot

## Page 21

15
mango hopper also  takes place.
Insecticides can be mixed in these
sprays for the joint control of
powdery mildew and hopper.
April
 If, blossom blight or anthracnose is
visible on the panicles, Carbendazim
(Bavistin @ 0.1% i.e. 19/1iter) should
be sprayed. In blossom blight, if
mixed infection is these with
Alteraria , spray of Companion
(Carbendazim + Mancozeb) is
recommended.
May
 Two to three sprays of Borax @ 1% is
desirable for the control of Black tip
or Internal necrosis during this
period. As the Borax is not easily
dissolved in ordinary cold water, it
should first be dissolved in small
quantity of warm water and then the
volume should be increased to the
desired quantity.
 For the control of latent infections on
fruit, 1-2 sprays of Thiophanate
methyle or Carbendazim (Topsin M
or Bavistin @ 0.1% i.e. 1g/liter) may
be done which will protect mango
fruits from post harvest diseases.
 For the control of sooty mould, spray
of a mixture of Wettable Sulphur +
Dimethoate + Gum acacia (0.2, 0.05
and 0.06% respectively) may be done.
 Indian Oil formulation (Tree spray
oil) is also effective at the
concentration of 3% for the control
of sooty mould.
 If there is a chance of bacterial canker
disease on fruit, Streptocycline 200
ppm should be sprayed.
June
 Second spray of Streptocycline 200
ppm may be done for the control of
bacterial canker disease.
July
 Spray of Copper-oxichloride @ 0.3%
i.e. 3g/liter may be done in the third
or fourth week for the control of
anthracnose and red rust.
 Sterilize the nursery soil by treating
soil with Formaldehyde and then
cover with polythene. Later,
polythene should be removed and
soil opened, so that the leftover
Formaldehyde is evaporated from
the soil before sowing the stone.
 The mango stones should also be
treated with Thiram or Captan @
0.3% and then sown.
 Application of Trichoderma  spp. in
the nursery soil for the control of root
diseases.
August
 Second and third sprays at the
interval of 15-20 days with copper
oxychloride @ 0.3% to protect the
crop from anthracnose and red rust.
 Field soil treatment with Captan
@0.3% for the control of seedling rots.
 Arrangement for the good drainage
of water in the nursery as it reduces
the chance of infection by root rot
fungi.
 Weeding should also be done during
this month so that the collateral hosts
of the Sclerotium  or  Rhizoctonia are
removed.
September
 One spray of Copper-oxichloride can
be repeated,  if there is more

## Page 22

16
incidence of anthracnose or red rust.
 Field cleaning and ploughing for the
control of the collateral hosts of
several pathogens.
October
 For the control of die back dried and
infected branches should be pruned
in such a way that it is removed 10
cm below the dried portion.
 After pruning, copper oxychloride
paste is applied to the cut ends in
nursery plants, while in case of
grown up plants copper oxychloride
is sprayed @ 0.3%. This spray also
takes care of phoma blight and
gummosis.
 For the control of gummosis, 200-
400g of copper sulphate can be
applied depending upon the age of
the plants.
 During this month, necessary
quantity of fertilizers should also be
applied, which will develop the
vigour of the plants and protect
plants from different diseases.
 For the control of malformation
disease of mango 200 ppm of
nepthalene acetic acid is sprayed in
the first week of October.
November
 Second and third sprays of Copper-
oxychloride @ 0.3% may be done for
the control of die back disease. This
spray also takes care of phoma blight.
December
 Protect crop from frost injury as
described in January.
 For the control of malformation,
deblossoming of new flower buds
should be done.
 All these operations are need based
and subject to the various disease
problems in different mango growing
areas.
